title: C10 training window v1 (ledger row -- storage -> continuum)
description: ONE ROW of the per-user training-window ledger, and the body of three of C10's four operations: `POST /training/windows {user_id}` (idempotent get-or-create of the user's open window), `POST /training/windows/{window_id}/close {user_id, outcome}`, and each element of `GET /training/windows?user_id=&state=` (which returns a bare JSON ARRAY of these -- the enumeration has no envelope, so a consumer validates it element-wise against this schema). A SIBLING FILE RATHER THAN AN EXTENSION OF the day-log schema, and the reason is the one already settled for C13: these are two different bodies on two different endpoints, and one schema could only carry both behind a `oneOf` that hides exactly the distinction the contract is about. c10_daylog.v1.json's $id names the day-log body specifically, and a consumer that validated 'a C10 day-log' against a root that had quietly become a union would be checking nothing. Two files, one contract -- C10 is a family of operations, not a single payload. VERSION 1, NOT 0, because it belongs to that family: C10 evolved in place (D18, 2026-07-26) from a raw C2 range read into the day-log fetch plus this ledger, keeping its number because its direction and peers are unchanged. NOTE WHAT THIS BODY DOES NOT CARRY, because its absence is the design: `last_trained_t`. The watermark is DERIVED -- MAX(t_end) over this user's rows with outcome == 'published' -- and never stored, which is what makes 'the watermark advances if and only if the cycle published' true by construction rather than by bookkeeping. There is no counter a close path could forget to leave alone and no second row that could disagree with the ledger. This body also carries no `contract`/`version` envelope, unlike C10's day-log body and C12/C14: it is a row, returned bare and returned in arrays, and stamping a contract tag on every element of an enumeration would put the envelope in the wrong place. The envelope-free shape is what storage serves today and this schema describes what is served, not what would have been tidier.

window_id.description: The window's identity: `w<YYYYMMDD>T<HHMMSS>Z`, derived from its END instant in UTC and minted in EXACTLY ONE PLACE. THE LENGTH BOUNDS ARE NOT REDUNDANT WITH THE PATTERN and must not be tidied away: `pattern` is unanchored-search semantics, and in the Python validator this contract is enforced by, `$` also matches just BEFORE A TRAILING NEWLINE -- so `w20260722T035900Z\n` satisfies the regex alone. That string is a different filesystem path from the id it looks like, and this is the same hole storage's own validator closes by using fullmatch rather than match. Pinning the width to exactly 17 closes it, and it independently states the fixed-width property that the lexicographic-ordering argument below actually rests on. OPAQUE -- consumers may compare it with < / >= and may do NOTHING else with it. In particular it is never parsed back into a date: under a [last_trained_t, now-delta) watermark there is no local date it could honestly name, because a window can span 23 h, 25 h or (after a missed night) 47 h. Three properties are load-bearing and none is decorative. (1) PATH-SAFE: continuum uses the id as a filesystem path component and an rmtree target (journal/, cycles/, reservoir/, adapters/), and a raw RFC3339 instant fails that gate on its colons. (2) LEXICOGRAPHIC ORDER == CHRONOLOGICAL ORDER: four continuum call sites compare these ids as plain strings and rely on nothing else, including the alias-monotonicity guard that must never move the serving alias backward; fixed width plus zero padding is what guarantees it. (3) SECOND GRANULARITY, NOT MINUTE: a truncating id can silently collide two distinct windows (a manual catch-up, a re-drive, a test), and one id collision corrupts the journal, the reservoir and C5 lineage at once. Collision is impossible by construction rather than by luck, because the ledger refuses to open a window whose end is not strictly greater than EVERY prior window end for that user -- not merely greater than the published watermark, since a gate-failed window's id occupies the id namespace too. It is a PER-USER token, which is why user_id rides beside it here and on every window-addressing surface.

user_id.description: The user whose ledger this row belongs to. Required on every window surface -- open, enumerate, close, and the day-log fetch -- because window_id is a per-user token derived from an instant: two users can legitimately open windows in the same second and therefore share an id, so a close keyed on the id alone would be a cross-user write to anyone who can guess a second. Isolation fails CLOSED: addressing someone else's window is a 404, never a report that the id names a row belonging to somebody else.

t_start.description: The window's UPDATED_AT lower bound, RFC3339 UTC, inclusive. It is this user's `last_trained_t` -- the end of their latest PUBLISHED window -- or, for a never-trained user, their earliest record. NOT an event time, NOT a local midnight, and NOT the extent of the content the window will render: membership is by updated_at, so a chunk captured Tuesday and uploaded Friday belongs to Friday's window and renders in a block anchored to Tuesday. Ingest time is the COMPLETENESS axis -- the only axis on which 'everything I had' is a guarantee -- which is why the training window sits on it while retraction ranges sit on event time. That asymmetry is deliberate and making the two agree would break one of them. IMMUTABLE ONCE OPENED.

t_end.description: The window's UPDATED_AT upper bound, RFC3339 UTC, exclusive: `now - delta`, truncated to the second so it agrees exactly with the window_id minted from it. `delta` (default 60 s) exists for exactly one reason -- an in-flight write racing the boundary could otherwise be assigned an updated_at below t_end yet commit AFTER materialization read the range. It is watermark lag, not slack, which is why it is service config and never a per-request knob a caller could shrink to zero. IMMUTABLE ONCE OPENED, and that is the property the idempotent open exists to protect: continuum's crash-safe journal is keyed by window_id, so a retry that recomputed `now` would mint a fresh id, a fresh journal, and therefore a full re-train, a second C5 entry and a second reservoir admission. Because late data cannot exist on this axis -- updated_at is assigned by storage at write, so nothing can land below an already-closed boundary -- no record is ever lost by closing here.

state.description: Where the row is in its only lifecycle. AT MOST ONE `open` window per user, enforced by a partial unique index rather than by the read-then-write in the get-or-create, because minting a second id for a user who already has one is precisely the failure the idempotent open exists to prevent. `consolidated` means the cycle REPORTED BACK -- whatever it reported. It does not mean the night succeeded; that is `outcome`'s job, and collapsing the two would make a gate failure indistinguishable from a publish at exactly the moment the difference matters.

outcome.description: What the cycle reported, or null while the window is still open. REQUIRED-NULLABLE (the key is always present, never omitted) so a reader never has to distinguish 'absent' from 'not yet' -- the same convention C2's segment `speaker` uses. EXACTLY ONE VALUE ADVANCES THE WATERMARK: `published`. Gate failure, freeze, crash, no data and too-little data all leave `last_trained_t` exactly where it was, so the NEXT window is a strict SUPERSET of the failed one -- the design-of-record's failed-day merge obtained structurally rather than by carry-over bookkeeping, which also makes a min-data floor nearly free (a below-floor night simply does not advance, and material accumulates until a run is worth it). `skipped_no_data` in particular does NOT advance; D18's first draft had it advance and that was corrected 2026-07-27. Named, accepted cost: an inactive user's open window grows and is re-scanned nightly, which is correct (there is nothing to train) and cheap at pilot scale. A CLOSED ENUM ON PURPOSE -- an unrecognised outcome must be a 422 at the edge, never a silent non-advance or, far worse, a silent advance. Strike counting is unaffected by the superset rule: each failed night is a distinct (larger) window, so each strikes once.

opened_at.description: RFC3339 UTC wall-clock instant this row was written. AUDIT ONLY: it is not t_start, it is not on the watermark axis, and no range arithmetic reads it. It sits `delta` plus however long the open took after t_end, and the gap between the two is the honest record of that lag.

closed_at.description: RFC3339 UTC instant the cycle reported its outcome, or null while the window is open. Nullable HERE and narrowed to a string by the `state == consolidated` branch below, rather than being declared a plain string: an open window has nothing to record, and a schema that demanded one would reject every row the open path mints. Required-nullable, like `outcome`, and it moves with it: re-closing with the SAME outcome is an idempotent retry that returns the row unchanged and does not move this timestamp, while re-closing with a DIFFERENT outcome is a 409 rather than a history rewrite -- if the new outcome were `published` it would silently advance a watermark that a failed night deliberately left alone.

allOf.description: An OPEN window has reported nothing, so it names no outcome and no close instant. Stated as a schema rule because it is the invariant the pydantic mirror cannot express: a row that is open AND carries an outcome would mean the ledger recorded a verdict for a window still accepting records, and if that outcome were `published` the derived watermark would already have advanced past a boundary the cycle had not finished.

A CONSOLIDATED window ALWAYS names its outcome and when it was recorded. This is the half that carries real weight: `last_trained_t` is derived by selecting rows whose outcome is `published`, so a consolidated row with a null outcome is not merely untidy -- it is a night whose training status is unanswerable, and it would be silently treated as non-advancing by a query that can only see what the column says.
